question: What are retained earnings?
model_answer_md:
The cumulative profit the company has made since it began, less everything it has paid out to shareholders as dividends.

$$\text{Closing RE} = \text{Opening RE} + \text{Net income} - \text{Dividends}$$

It sits within equity on the balance sheet, and it is the line that connects the income statement to the balance sheet: each year's net income flows into it, which is why a walkthrough always ends by moving retained earnings.

The common misunderstanding is worth pre-empting: retained earnings are **not a pot of cash**. The profits were retained, but they have since been spent on inventory, equipment or repaying debt. Kestrel could have large retained earnings and very little cash.
key_points: Cumulative net income since inception, less cumulative dividends
Sits within equity on the balance sheet
The link that carries net income onto the balance sheet
Not a cash balance — the profits have been reinvested
Closing RE = opening RE + net income − dividends

follow_ups.question: Can retained earnings be negative?
follow_ups.answer_md: Yes — it is then usually called an accumulated deficit, and it means cumulative losses and distributions have exceeded cumulative profits. Common for young, loss-making companies, and it does not by itself signal distress if the business is well funded by share issuance.

follow_ups.question: How exactly does it link to net income?
follow_ups.answer_md: Directly and every period: net income is added to retained earnings, and dividends are subtracted. That is why, in any three-statement walkthrough, the change in retained earnings equals the change in net income whenever no dividend is paid.

weak_answer_note: Describes retained earnings as cash held back, or cannot state the roll-forward formula.
